identity.title: The strongest cool core in REXCESS: Missing X-ray cavities in RXC J2014.8-2430

paper_type_evidence.quote: We present a broad, multi-wavelength study of RXC J2014.8-2430, the most extreme cool-core cluster in the Representative *XMM-Newton* Cluster Structure Survey (REXCESS), using *Chandra* X-ray, Southern Astrophysical Research (SOAR) Telescope spectroscopic and narrow-band imaging, Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA)
Through the ALMA Cycle 7 project 2018.1.00940.S, the central region of RXC J2014.8-2430 was observed in Band 3 with the 12-metre ‘main’ array of ALMA.

question.value: Why are bilateral X-ray cavities and radio bubbles missing in RXC J2014.8-2430 despite it being an extreme cool-core cluster hosting a powerful radio source, and how does sloshing affect the cool gas reservoir?

evidence.quote: the *Chandra* imaging observations surprisingly do not reveal the bi-lateral X-ray cavities one might expect to see in the intracluster medium (ICM) of an extreme cool core hosting a powerful radio source
ALMA observations of the CO(1-0) emission reveal a large reservoir of molecular gas that traces the extended H$\alpha$ emission in the direction of the cool core.

findings_qualitative.value: Chandra imaging does not reveal bilateral X-ray cavities in the ICM despite the cluster hosting a powerful radio source and having a strong cool core.

evidence.quote: the *Chandra* imaging observations surprisingly do not reveal the bi-lateral X-ray cavities one might expect to see in the intracluster medium (ICM) of an extreme cool core hosting a powerful radio source

findings_qualitative.value: ALMA CO(1-0) observations reveal a large molecular gas reservoir co-spatial with the extended H-alpha emission, with a bimodal velocity distribution in the core and a south-western spur.

evidence.quote: Fig. [13](#fig:Halpha_and_CO) (upper panel) shows the molecular gas traced by CO emission to be co-spatial with the warmer gas traced by H$\alpha$ emission

The second row of Fig. [14](#fig:alma_co_regions) reveal there is a significant bimodality to the molecular gas velocity distribution for the CO(1-0) emission superposed on the BCG, while the brightest singular offset feature corresponds to the south-west extension tracing the H$\alpha$ spur (third row).

findings_qualitative.value: The radio, mm, and optical AGN peaks are co-located but offset by 3.5'' (9.4 kpc) to the east of the X-ray peak due to sloshing.

findings_qualitative.value: The cluster core has a strongly peaked metallicity profile and low central entropy, indicating the cool core remains intact and sloshing near the core is likely subsonic.

evidence.quote: We argue that the sloshing near the core is likely subsonic, as expected, given the co-location of the H$\alpha$, CO(1-0), radio continuum, and stellar emission peaks and their proximity to the X-ray peak. Further, the X-ray emission from the core is strongly concentrated, as is the distribution of metals, indicating the cool core remains largely intact.

claims.hypothesis: Extreme cool-core clusters with powerful central radio sources should exhibit detectable X-ray cavities and radio bubbles.
claims.experiment: Analyzed 20 ks Chandra X-ray imaging (unsharp masking, 2D beta-model subtraction, and 3D toy cavity modeling) along with VLA 1.4 GHz and GMRT 610 MHz radio images.
claims.result: No obvious X-ray cavities or radio bubbles are detected; toy models show small (< 6'') cavities could hide if aligned along the line of sight at > 20 kpc from the core, or if obscured by sloshing edges.
claims.finding: Either the cavities are nearly aligned with the line of sight, or sloshing has displaced the fuel supply and preempted the AGN feedback cycle (or the AGN has only recently turned on).

evidence.quote: We conclude either that the radio source and its cavities in the X-ray gas are nearly aligned along the line of sight, or that ram pressure induced by sloshing has significantly displaced the cool molecular gas feeding it, perhaps preempting the AGN feedback cycle.

With an expected cavity lifetime of less than 100 million years, it is possible for cavities on the smaller end ($<$ 6$\ensuremath{''}$) of the expected size to exist in this cluster along our line of sight without being detected in the X-ray image.

claims.hypothesis: ICM sloshing near the cluster core entrains and influences the spatial and velocity distribution of the cold molecular and warm atomic gas.
claims.experiment: Compared ALMA CO(1-0) intensity and kinematics with SOAR H-alpha narrow-band imaging, Goodman spectroscopy, and Chandra X-ray temperature/surface brightness maps, and estimated ram pressure.
claims.result: CO(1-0) and H-alpha are co-spatial with a flat radial ratio, extend along a south-western spur toward the offset X-ray peak, share a velocity component between the BCG core and the spur, and experience ram pressure (>= 4.1 x 10^-10 erg cm^-3) comparable to thermal pressure.
claims.finding: Sloshing motion influences and likely entrains the cold molecular and warm atomic gas reservoir.

evidence.quote: The comparable levels of thermal pressure and ram pressure $P_{\rm ram}$ support the idea that the sloshing motion could be a factor influencing the observed spatial distribution of the cold molecular and warm atomic gas.

Since one component of the velocity in the core is at the same velocity at the dominant component in the south-western spur, we argue that this supports the notion the molecular gas distribution is being influenced by the sloshing near the core.

claims.hypothesis: The positive radio residual west-northwest of the central source in the GMRT 610 MHz image represents a genuine radio bubble.
claims.experiment: Examined ALMA CO(1-0) emission in the western spur region corresponding to the GMRT 610 MHz positive residual.
claims.result: CO(1-0) emission in the western region is much less significant (M_mol ~ 0.16 x 10^9 M_sun) and shows no evidence for entrainment by a radio bubble.
claims.finding: The extended western radio feature in the GMRT data is most likely spurious.

evidence.quote: Notably, the CO(1-0) emission to the west (fourth row of Fig. [14](#fig:alma_co_regions)), where the radio residual seen in the GMRT data is located (see Fig. [5](#fig:radio)), is much less significant and does not provide any evidence for entrainment by a putative radio bubble. We therefore favour the interpretation that the extended radio feature in the GMRT data is most likely spurious.

why_this_data.value: ALMA Band 3 observations were performed to probe the location and dynamics of cold molecular gas via CO(1-0) and compare with optical H-alpha, radio, and X-ray structures.

evidence.quote: We use millimetre-wave observations performed by ALMA on December 24, 2018, to probe the location and dynamics of the molecular gas traced by the lowest transition of the dominant form of carbon monoxide, CO(1-0)
For comparison with the optical data, we turn to the view ALMA provides of the cold molecular gas, as traced by CO(1-0).

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Foreground CO(1-0) absorption causing the central dip in the CO spectrum was considered and discounted because a two-Gaussian emission fit yields reduced chi^2 = 1.05 and known CO absorption dips are only a few percent against continuum.

evidence.quote: While the possibility exists that the observed dip could be due to CO(1-0) absorption from foreground molecular gas, we discount this possibility as the emission is well-described by the fitting of two Gaussian profiles, with a reduced $\chi^2=1.05$.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: A rotating disk or bilateral bubbles pushing gas to explain the optical velocity gradient were rejected because the velocity structure is one-sided and lacks a two-peaked profile.

evidence.quote: The optical velocity structure does not appear to be due to a rotating disk, since it is one-sided and the disk would have to be off-centre from the peak of the emission, even though the emission peaks are aligned.

Additionally, the optical emission is inconsistent with a pair of bubbles pushing the emission-line gas in front of each one because that would produce a profile with two peaks if the gas is otherwise optically thin.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Suppression of existing X-ray cavities by strong sloshing was rejected because timescales are >= 0.5 Gyr, no radio mini-halo is observed, and the low-entropy, metal-peaked cool core remains intact.

evidence.quote: The lack of a radio mini-halo, the compact distribution of metals in the core, and the strong, luminous, low-entropy cool core all indicate the sloshing near the core is too weak to significantly disrupt any putative bubbles

limitations_admitted.value: Moment maps of CO(1-0) are not corrected for beam smearing effects.

evidence.quote: We note that the moment maps are not corrected for beam smearing effects, as they are largely being used to gauge the phenomenological behaviour of the cold gas.

limitations_admitted.value: Bright central AGN causes dynamic range limitations and residual sidelobes in both VLA and GMRT radio images.

evidence.quote: Due to dynamic range limitations ($\sim 2500$ in this image), residual sidelobes from the strong central radio source in RXC J2014.8-2430 are a dominant contribution to the central background noise, raising the local noise by a factor of two.

However, the bright central AGN in both of the radio images leads to dynamic range issues, so that much of the structure left after modelling the sources could be dominated by residuals due to imperfect phase calibration.

limitations_admitted.value: Cannot distinguish whether the optical velocity gradient indicates gas infall or outflow, and only radial velocities are measured rather than true 3D sloshing speeds.

evidence.quote: However, we cannot distinguish whether the velocity gradient is indicative of gas infall or outflow.
Since we only measure radial velocities of the line, the true 3D sloshing speed could be somewhat higher.
